newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila waterworks bidding said going smoothly.
newsitem.headline: Manila waterworks bidding said going smoothly.

text.p: The privatisation of the Manila waterworks system, which has been dogged by controversy and litigation, is proceeding smoothly, government officials and bidding companies said on Thursday.

The bids for two 25-year contracts to operate the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), which may cost the winners up to $7.0 billion, have been threatened by a court case and news reports that one of the four bidders had submitted a flawed offer.
But officials said the process was steaming ahead.
"We have been quite careful. We are now in the final stages of the bidding. And so far, there has been no question up to this point," MWSS administrator Angel Lazaro III told a news conference.

The four consortia submitted bids for the contracts on January 6. Their offers will be evaluated by a technical committee and the financial bids of those groups which are cleared will be opened on January 23.

The four groups include Ayala Corp with Bechtel Corp of the United States and United Utilities plc ; Lyonnaise des Eaux SA with Benpres Holdings Corp ; Anglian Water Plc with Australia Water Technologies Pty Ltd and Metro Pacific Corp ; and Compangnie Generale des Eaux with Aboitiz Equity Ventures Inc.
The MWSS summoned the bidders to a meeting on Wednesday to clarify some points in their technical bids.

Earlier this week, a newspaper reported that the bid of the Ayala-led consortium was flawed and the government was debating whether to disqualify the group or to scrap the present bidding and restart the process from scratch.
But Lazaro denied the report, saying: "The technical evaluation is ongoing. It's not finished yet."

Ayala Property Management Corp president Antonio Aquino said Wednesday's meeting was not meant to discuss only Ayala's bid, but questions were also raised on the technical bids submitted by other bidders.
Earlier, even before the bids were submitted, businessmen building a dam east of Manila had sought to stop the process, saying that the privatisation would render their project unviable.
The next court hearing is set for Monday, three days before the opening of the financial bids. Lazaro declined to comment on the case, saying it was for the court to decide.
When asked whether the pending court case had discouraged prospective bidders from the contest, Ayala's Aquino said: "That (litigation) is always the risk that you will have in any bidding."
Aboitiz vice president Jose Luis Romero-Salas said the bidding had been handled professionally. But he did not discount the possibility of a legal delay.
"Anybody who feels that he has been unduly prejudiced will always seek legal recourse," he said.
Another possible glitch which might muddle the process is the fate of the MWSS workers whose jobs might be jeopardised following the privatisation.

Only 3,500 of MWSS's 5,500 workers will be needed by the concessionaires, but Lazaro said any workers laid off would be provided for by the MWSS and the concessionaires through attractive incentive packages.
